claim: Larger LLMs are well-calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false questions when prompted in the right format, and can self-evaluate open-ended answers via a 'P(True)' probability that improves further when considering multiple of the model's own samples before judging validity.
stance_target: whether verbalized/self-evaluated confidence tracks correctness in general LLMs
scope_conditions: General QA/multiple-choice/true-false tasks; whole-answer granularity; Anthropic models of varying scale
quoted_support: We find encouraging performance, calibration, and scaling for P(True) on a diverse array of tasks. Performance at self-evaluation further improves when we allow models to consider many of their own samples before predicting the validity of one specific possibility.

claim: P(IK) (probability 'I Know'), a confidence estimate trained without reference to a specific proposed answer, partially generalizes across tasks but struggles with calibration on genuinely new/held-out tasks.
stance_target: the idea that trained self-report confidence transfers cleanly to new domains without degradation
scope_conditions: General QA tasks, cross-task generalization setting
quoted_support: Models perform well at predicting P(IK) and partially generalize across tasks, though they struggle with calibration of P(IK) on new tasks.

claim: This paper is a foundational precedent for optimistic 'LLMs mostly know what they know' framing at whole-answer granularity in general QA, not code, and does not compare a hidden-state linear probe against verbalized confidence -- its P(True)/P(IK) mechanisms are themselves forms of model self-report, not an independent internal-probe baseline.
stance_target: the AAAI-27 pivot's novelty claim that per-requirement code probe-vs-verbalization is underexplored
scope_conditions: General QA, whole-answer granularity, self-report methods only (no external linear probe)
quoted_support: We hope these observations lay the groundwork for training more honest models, and for investigating how honesty generalizes to cases where models are trained on objectives other than the imitation of human writing.
